name: Meroitic
confidence_why: Meroitic survives only in writing, and the one author to propose stress placements, Rowan (2006, 2015), states that the stress assignment "can only be speculated" and reconstructs it word by word from Egyptian and Coptic etymologies (penultimate in asori, abr and amni, initial in ar, ant and xansa), while Rilly (2003, 2016, 2020), Zyhlarz (1930) and Peust (1999) say nothing about Meroitic stress.

Zeitschrift für Ägyptische Sprache und Altertumskunde 142(1): 70-84. doi:10.1515/zaes-2015-0007 (SOAS eprint 19169, version of record). Same argument in Rowan, Kirsty. 2006. catalog_locator: pp.77-78, sec. 2.1 'Pretonic loss of Meroitic a' and sec. 2.2 'Meroitic forms with no loss of a', incl. fn.57 and fn.59. Thesis (Rowan 2006) cross-checks (page numbers): ch.3 sec.2.1 p.196 ('obviously cannot be exactly detailed'); ch.4 sec.1.2.1 p.221 ('resultantly the stress is on the initial syllable'); ch.4 sec.1.2.2 p.222 (/'xansa/, 'attracted to heavy syllables').
catalog_quote: The stress assignment of Meroitic forms can only be speculated although there are common variant forms where the Meroitic sign a is frequently omitted and these forms are suggestive for proposals on the placement of stress. It is claimed here that the omission of a in Meroitic is due to its pretonic position in the word. When a is not in a pretonic position, there is no omission of this sign. ... The Meroitic stress is on the penultimate syllable [ʔaˈsuri], this means that a [ʔa] is in pretonic position and consequently is subject to aphaeresis. This results in the later written form sori [ˈsuri]. ... The third form in (11c) above, ant ~ at "Priest", is interesting as evidence is put forward to show that the placement of stress is on the first syllable of the archaic and late forms. ... (12) ant /ˈʔanata/ > /ˈʔanəta/ > /ˈʔanta/ = at. The vowel weakening of the penultimate syllable can be explained by it being in an unstressed (post-tonic) position, i.e. the stress is on the antepenultimate (first) syllable /ˈʔanata/ > /ˈʔanəta/ > /ˈʔanta/. ... [fn. 57] Rilly 2007, 395 defines this neutralisation as taking place during the first century CE. He also proposes that the reduction of this vowel is probably due to the positioning of the vowel in the word or to the force of tonic stress. ... [fn. 59] Furthermore, stress in general is attracted to heavy syllables, i.e. those containing a consonant in coda position e.g. CVC(C).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Extinct, script-only language: no general word-stress rule is recoverable. Rowan infers that Meroitic had a dynamic (stress) accent from (i) 1st-c. CE loss of word-initial a only when pretonic and (ii) post-tonic vowel reduction/syncope to schwa/zero, and reconstructs stress word by word from Egyptian/Coptic/Greek equivalents: penultimate in asori 'Osiris', abr 'man', amni 'Amun', ar 'Horus'; initial (antepenultimate) in ant~at 'priest'. Rilly 2007:395 (reported) likewise attributes the /a/>/ə/>zero neutralisation to vowel position or 'the force of tonic stress' without fixing its place.
new_statements.exceptions: Initial a is retained even if pretonic when deletion would put /r/ word-initially (ar 'Horus', arome 'Rome'; Rilly 2007:287 fn.5 phonotactic ban on initial r); apheresis of amni seems blocked after a preceding word-final e (Griffith 1911:71, Rilly 2007:303); fn.59 'stress in general is attracted to heavy syllables'. Most diagnosed items are Egyptian loans/theonyms whose Meroitic stress is argued to fossilise the Egyptian stress position.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level (isolated lexical items/theonyms/titles as written in inscriptions); evidence is orthographic variation across early vs late texts plus foreign transcriptions, not citation-form phonetics. Rowan's a = [ʔa] (CV) analysis differs from Rilly's (a = bare initial vowel), but both treat the loss as prosodic/pretonic.
new_statements.identity_note: Meroitic (mero1237, ISO xmr), the written language of the Kingdom of Kush/Meroe (c. 300 BCE-450 CE), known only from inscriptions in the Meroitic cursive and hieroglyphic alphasyllabary; Glottolog lists it as an isolate, Rilly classifies it as Northern East Sudanic (Nilo-Saharan). All stress claims are reconstructions from orthographic variation (early vs late texts) and Egyptian/Coptic/Greek transcriptions, largely of loanwords and theonyms; no dialect distinction is made.
